scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9104: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports they have completely
lost connectivity to the partner network -- they cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2) in
the peer AS since this morning. The team is convinced their own edge router,
router1, has fallen over and want router1 restarted. Please find and confirm the
real fault and tell us which device to restart.

injection.action: kill the BGP routing daemon (and its watchdog) on router2

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth0 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on router2: its BGP routing daemon (bgpd) has been killed, so
the eBGP session between router1 and router2 drops and the inter-AS prefixes are
no longer exchanged. With no route to the peer AS, pc1 (195.11.14.2) cannot reach
pc2 (200.1.1.2). The ticket MISDIRECTS to router1 (the user's own edge router),
but the fault is on the PEER side: router2 is the eBGP speaker whose daemon is
dead. router1 is healthy -- its bgpd is still running and its inter-AS interface
is up; it simply has no session because router2 stopped speaking BGP.

The correct diagnosis identifies router2 (bgpd down) as the faulty device and
explicitly EXONERATES router1: router1's BGP daemon and interfaces are fine, so
the user's "router1 has fallen over" hypothesis is wrong. An agent that restarts
/ blames router1 has followed the ticket's misdirection instead of the evidence.

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): bgpd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router bgp` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists bgpd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the bgp configuration is missing/empty on router2" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart FRR/bgpd on router2 (`service frr restart`). Once bgpd is running again,
the eBGP session to router1 re-establishes, router2 re-learns and re-advertises
the inter-AS prefixes, and pc1 reaches pc2 normally. router1 needs no change.
scoring_axes: must-identify-bgpd-down: identifies bgpd on router2 is down (the peer eBGP speaker), not a fault on router1
bonus-exonerates-router1: notes router1's bgpd is up and its inter-AS interface is healthy, rejecting the ticket's "router1 fell over" hypothesis

agent.diagnosis_text:
The BGP daemon (bgpd) on router2 has crashed and is no longer running, which is
the sole cause of the total connectivity loss between pc1 and pc2.

Affected component: The bgpd process of the FRR routing stack on router2.

Mechanism: With bgpd dead on router2, no BGP session can be established on that
side. Router1's bgpd is fully healthy and correctly configured (AS 1, peer
193.10.11.2 remote-as 2), but it is stuck in the "Active" state — repeatedly
trying to open a TCP connection to port 179 on router2 and finding nothing
listening. As a result, neither router has BGP-learned routes: router1 has no
route to 200.1.1.0/24 (pc2's subnet) and router2 has no route to 195.11.14.0/24
(pc1's subnet). Router1 returns "Destination Net Unreachable" ICMP for every
packet pc1 sends toward pc2.

Localization: The fault is entirely on router2. The FRR log confirms bgpd was
alive at startup, briefly established a session at 14:12:38, exchanged updates
with router1, and then crashed at 14:14:07 — ZEBRA logged "Client 'bgp'
encountered an error and is shutting down" and immediately withdrew the 1 BGP
route from its RIB. The process list on router2 shows zebra, mgmtd, and staticd
running but no bgpd. /etc/frr/daemons has bgpd=yes and /etc/frr/frr.conf
contains the correct BGP stanza (router bgp 2, neighbor 193.10.11.1 remote-as 1,
network 200.1.1.0/24), so this is a daemon crash, not a configuration absence.

Root cause: bgpd on router2 crashed after lab startup and was never restarted by
watchfrr, leaving the BGP peering permanently broken.

Corrective fix: Restart bgpd (or the entire FRR stack) on router2 — e.g.,
`service frr restart` inside the router2 container. Do NOT restart router1; it is
completely healthy. Once bgpd on router2 recovers, the eBGP session will
re-establish within seconds and prefix exchange will restore full pc1↔pc2
reachability.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states bgpd on router2 has crashed/is not running, localizes the fault to router2, and exonerates router1 as healthy.

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerates-router1: notes router1's bgpd is up and its inter-AS interface is healthy, rejecting the ticket's "router1 fell over" hypothesis
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states router1's bgpd is healthy and its inter‑AS interface is up (router1 is 'completely healthy'), rejecting the ticket's 'router1 fell over' hypothesis.
Recommends restarting bgpd (or service frr) on router2 to restore the eBGP session, which matches the expected fix.

The agent's logs show explicit evidence (router2 'bgpd is not running', no bgpd in ps, /etc/frr/frr.conf contains BGP stanza, frr.log shows bgpd crash, router1 BGP in Active state and no learned routes) that directly supports the conclusion that router2's bgpd crashed and caused the outage. The inferences follow logically and the investigation covered the necessary checks to rule out alternatives and exonerate router1.
